competitors.name: Enterprise Community Partners - Faith-Based Development Initiative (FBDI)
competitors.what_they_do: National nonprofit program, running since 2006, that helps congregations turn land into affordable housing. It offers grants for market studies, feasibility analyses and pre-development, a development curriculum, project-specific technical assistance, peer cohorts, loans and equity, and policy advocacy. It also publishes a free 7-step Faith-Based Development Guide and a 'Good Futures Accelerator' that helps a house of worship assess whether development is realistic. This is the free or grant-funded version of the idea's Land Options Report.
competitors.scale_or_funding: About $6.6M in grants, 2,000+ affordable homes created or preserved, 9,000+ units in the pipeline, and $211M in loans and equity. It reaches 16 jurisdictions in 9 states as of 2026, and a COGIC collaboration aims to train 200 congregations. Philanthropy-backed (source: enterprisecommunity.org FBDI page and the Sept 2026 '20 years of FBDI' story, https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/story/20-years-enterprises-faith-based-development-initiative).

competitors.name: YIGBY(R) Housing (San Diego 501(c)(3), born from Catalyst of San Diego & Imperial Counties)
competitors.what_they_do: Nonprofit 'integrated, repeatable platform' for turning faith-community land into permanently affordable housing. Its site has separate tracks for congregations, denominational leaders and philanthropic investors, plus a self-assessment tool, a resource center, a state-by-state YIGBY legislation map, a partner network and events. Its first project, Bethel One (26 units on Bethel AME land in Logan Heights, San Diego), reached completion in mid-2026. It is the closest match to the idea's buyer, because it already courts denominational bodies.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Self-reported: 134-unit pipeline, $8.8M in assets managed, $16M capital formation in progress. Denominational partners named on the site are AME District 2, the Episcopal Diocese of San Diego and the Pacifica ELCA Synod. The board includes a Bridge Investment Group co-founder and a GoFundMe co-founder. The site is built on the Base44 no-code platform, which suggests a small team. Sources: https://yigby.org and its JS bundle, plus https://www.kpbs.org/news/local/2024/01/08/san-diegos-first-affordable-housing-project-on-church-land-under-construction and https://www.10news.com/news/local-news/logan-heights-church-set-to-open-26-affordable-housing-units-for-veterans-and-seniors-in-san-diego

competitors.name: Rooted Good (Good Futures Accelerator; institutional resources for denominations)
competitors.what_they_do: Helps congregations generate income from buildings and land: social enterprise, using and developing property for revenue and ministry, and aligning money and mission. It runs the Good Futures Accelerator, offers how-to guides, and has a separate 'institutional resources' track for organizations that support churches. Its site has a 2-minute quiz that recommends building and land options. It covers the 'what can our property become' question at a lighter, coaching level.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Not disclosed on the fetched pages. It appears to be a nonprofit or philanthropy-backed intermediary and lists no pricing. Enterprise's guide page points congregations to the Good Futures Accelerator as an early-stage resource (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/faith-based-development-guide).

competitors.name: Terner Center (UC Berkeley) faith and college land mapping
competitors.what_they_do: Free public research that maps parcel-level housing potential on faith-owned and college land. It found 171,000+ potentially developable acres statewide in California, including 4,675 acres in San Diego County. This commoditizes the 'parcel and zoning analysis' half of the Land Options Report, at least for California.
competitors.scale_or_funding: University research center; the reports are free. The earlier 2020 mapping paper is at https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/faith-based-housing-development/

competitors.name: Partners for Sacred Places
competitors.what_they_do: National nonprofit that helps congregations keep and reuse historic buildings. It advises on shared space, capital campaigns and 'transitioning your space', and reports congregations raising $13.5M through its help. Its fetched pages show no housing or land-sale programs, but it is a trusted advisor to the same board members.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Nonprofit; consulting and training, funding details not on the fetched page.

competitors.name: LISC, UCC Church Building & Loan Fund, Oikos Institute, Wesley Theological Seminary (named ecosystem intermediaries)
competitors.what_they_do: Enterprise's Radical Common Sense podcast page names these as intermediaries and support organizations for faith-based development: LISC (community development intermediary), the UCC Church Building & Loan Fund (denominational lender), Oikos Institute (training) and Wesley Seminary (fellowships). I could not load their own sites, so their exact offerings are unverified. LISC's homepage shows no dedicated faith-land program.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established nonprofits and denominational bodies. LISC is a national intermediary; the others' scale was not verified.

white_space:
Search budget note: the WebSearch quota (200/200) was spent before I started, so this verdict rests on direct page fetches, not the planned 6-12 searches. I could not check Crunchbase, Product Hunt, YC or TechCrunch. A GitHub repository search for open-source YIGBY or zoning tools returned 0 results. The unsearched areas most likely to hold competitors are (a) for-profit church-property brokers, (b) church-property law firms and (c) parcel and zoning SaaS vendors that could add a faith-land filter. Treat 'no venture-backed direct startup found' as unconfirmed.

What is crowded: the housing-on-faith-land advisory layer. Enterprise FBDI (20 years, philanthropy-funded), YIGBY Housing (San Diego) and Rooted Good offer free or grant-funded feasibility support, and Terner publishes free parcel mapping. A $1.5-3k Land Options Report would compete with free or subsidised equivalents, and Enterprise grants can pay for the market studies and feasibility analyses that the report would replace.

What remains unserved, in my fetches at least:
1. Denomination-specific governance and disposition process. Enterprise's guide page did not describe denominational approvals. It is a productized 'approval-path map' per polity (trust clause and canon-law thresholds, donor-restricted funds and cemeteries, state attorney-general notice). It also covers non-housing exits such as merger, sale to another congregation, and mixed use. Existing players are development-biased and lead with housing. This overlaps with denominational property offices and church-property attorneys, so it is a service wedge, not a technology moat.
2. Portfolio-level triage for judicatories. Screening an entire diocese, conference or synod portfolio of hundreds of parcels against each state's law, then sorting into hold, merge, ground-lease, sell or housing candidates. I found no productized offering for this. Enterprise and YIGBY work project by project.
3. States where the by-right rules allow mixed-income and land value is positive. The following comes from YIGBY's own legislation map, which is partly LLM-generated, so verify each item. Virginia SB 388 (signed 22 Apr 2026) requires only 60% affordable units at 80% AMI for 30+ years, plus 70% residential floor area. Florida HB 1389 was signed 26 Jun 2026 and took effect 1 Jul 2026, but the Florida Senate page did not confirm its religious-land provisions. YIGBY Housing is San Diego-centred, and Enterprise's Southeast RFQ signals it is only now qualifying consultants in Atlanta and South Florida.

Core thesis problem (verified against the bill text at https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB4): California SB 4 requires 100% of units (excluding manager units) to be lower-income, up to 20% moderate-income and up to 5% staff. It requires 55-year rental deed restrictions, requires that the religious institution owned the land on or before 1 Jan 2024, and sunsets 1 Jan 2036. So the idea's insight that 'residual land value often exceeds the building's as-is price' is doubtful in California. Deed-restricted affordable land is worth little without subsidy, and a sale to an investor forfeits the by-right path. Bethel One cost about $260k per unit and was financed privately (KPBS link above). The land-value arbitrage may hold only in mixed-income states such as Virginia, or via ground-lease rent to a mission developer.
evidence_of_demand:
Real need is well documented; willingness to pay a for-profit is not.

Need and spend, all from philanthropic or nonprofit actors:
- Enterprise's FBDI has run for 20 years and reports $6.6M in grants, $211M in loans and equity, 9,000+ pipeline units and 16 jurisdictions in 9 states. Its grants explicitly fund market studies, feasibility analyses and pre-development support. https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/impact-areas/preservation-and-production/faith-based-development and https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/story/20-years-enterprises-faith-based-development-initiative
- Enterprise's podcast page lists the barriers congregations face: they are 'land rich and cash poor', pastors lack real-estate training, projects are complex, and there is 'substantial demand for technical assistance'. https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/radical-common-sense-david-bowers
- Terner Center: 171,000+ developable acres of faith and college land in California. https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/faith-based-and-college-land-housing/
- YIGBY Housing self-reports a 134-unit pipeline, $16M of capital formation in progress, and denominational partners (Episcopal Diocese of San Diego, AME District 2, Pacifica ELCA Synod), so judicatories do engage intermediaries. https://yigby.org
- Policy tailwind: OR SB 8 (2021), WA HB 1377 (2019), CA SB 4 (2023, text verified on leginfo), MN (2023), MD (2024), and 2026 laws in VA and FL. The Virginia, Maryland, Oregon, Washington and Minnesota items come from YIGBY's own legislation map and are unverified. Enterprise confirms Columbus and Virginia passed supportive legislation. The Florida bill's status was confirmed, but its religious-land provisions were not (https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/1389).

What I did not find: any evidence that congregations or judicatories pay $1.5-3k for a land-options report, any RFP for such a report, or any paid comparable. Existing spend is grant-funded technical assistance, and free reports and tools set a low price anchor. Judicatory bulk contracts of $25-60k per year are unproven. Closure and decline statistics were not retrieved: the Lifeway page returned 404 and no independent source was fetched.
kill_reason: n/a. Not killed because a narrow wedge remains: a denomination-specific governance and disposition playbook plus portfolio-level triage for judicatories, focused on states where by-right rules allow mixed-income. Two cautions apply. First, the headline 'faith-land housing options report' is already free or grant-funded (Enterprise FBDI, YIGBY Housing, Terner mapping), so the original pitch as written would be killed. Second, the search budget was exhausted, so for-profit startups, church-property brokers and law firms were not checked.
sharper_angle:
Drop the consumer-facing 'Land Options Report for a 50-250 member congregation' and drop the California-first plan. Instead, sell an annual 'Portfolio Disposition Desk' to judicatories (dioceses, conferences, synods, presbyteries). It has three parts.

1. Screen every parcel in the body's portfolio against state faith-land laws and local zoning. Start with mixed-income by-right states such as Virginia (60% affordable), and validate Florida and Maryland, rather than California's 100%-affordable SB 4.
2. Pre-map each polity's approval path: trust clause, canon or polity thresholds, donor-restricted funds and cemeteries, attorney-general notice, historic designation. Attach member-vote and communication scripts. Cover all exits: hold, merge, ground lease, sell, or mixed use with a retained chapel.
3. Hand the housing-viable sites to existing nonprofit developers and intermediaries (Enterprise FBDI, YIGBY, LISC-backed developers) and to for-profit developers under a referral or site-sourcing arrangement, so you are not competing with the free tier. Be careful with contingent fees: broker licensing and unauthorised-practice-of-law rules apply, so use flat fees and an attorney partner.

The differentiator is the approval-path knowledge base per denomination and the portfolio-scale triage, not the parcel analysis. Before building, confirm with 5-10 judicatory property officers whether they already pay law firms or brokers for this, and check the for-profit and startup landscape that was not searched here.
